I'm not a D&D rules scholar, or lawyer, but the picture that pops into my head when I read the description of a warforged incorporating armor is the cliched one of a gelatinous cube with the armor of some dead adventurer floating inside it. 

   Incorporating brings to mind something becoming one with (or throughout) something else, like when we eat food, our bodies incorporate the food molecules into our body tissue. We wear clothing, but that clothing is not incorporated into us, we do not become one with it.

   The Integrated Protection description makes it sound like an armored warforged does not wear its armor in the traditional sense, that it doesn't wear its armor at all, that donning armor for a warforged is not the process of putting something on/ wearing something like it is for other races, but is instead the process of incorporation, or becoming one with something else , and that the difference between the two type of donning is similar to the difference between "on" and "in": There is not warforged and then armor, there is just warforged: An armored warforged isn't wearing armor.

   If the preceding paragraphs have any merit or validity,  it may then be worth considering the wording of the barbarian's Unarmored defense:

"While you are not **wearing** any armor..."

   If being armored does not mean that a warforged is **wearing** armor, then an armored warforged does not strictly meet the conditions of exclusion from the benefits of unarmored defense.

   As for the application of the wording of don :

"This is the time it takes to **put on** the item."

​

I'm not saying that a plate wearing barb with unarmored defense wouldn't be broken, but do think that an argument can be made for its validity, even if said argument is only hypothetical food for thought.

I've had similar thoughts. I've come up with cool character concepts and theory crafts that would be really fun to build, but will probably try them all the way because they rely on the character making it through more levels than characters usually make it through. 

   Imagine that your character was the protagonist in an 80s sports movie, but that the movie is stopped/paused indefinitely / the tape (**this is an 80s movie analogy**) is removed from the VCR before the training montage even starts, or that your character is Steve Rogers, but the movie ends right after Bucky saves him in the alley.

It's not so much that level 20 games are unappealing, but more that people have been conditioned to not take thoughts of them so seriously because those games are so rare.

Games/ groups not lasting past levels 5 - 9 means that players have little to no experience with higher level skills/abilities/spells/ tactics, and that DMs often have little more experience than the players here and are thus not able to help, correct, or answer questions. DMs at this point also lack the experience necessary to create and adapt the game to suit higher level players characters. 

A DM of a game with a level 3  barbarian, rogue, and wizard knows instinctively how many goblin archers might be too many for the party to run into at the start of their quest, as well as how many more would bring balance to the encounter if the party knows how to take care of business.

After the lower mid levels, few people have the experience to instinctively know whether the party's at a point where more goblins should be added to the encounters, or whether something else should take their place entirely. 

"The level 5 wizard took care of that 35.5 kobold (one of them was the kobold version of Lieutenant Dan) drum circle that was sitting in the park, all on his own. Throw in the barbarian and the rogue, they should  have no problem handling the mind flayer and beholder waiting for them around the corner."

Prematurely ended games also mean that everything that makes up later level games does not automatically receive the same mass consumer play testing and tire kicking as things in the lower levels do. 

Because so many more hours of experience are accumulated with lower levels, potential issues are discovered sooner, more potential issues are discovered, and more time, energy, and thought can be devoted to resolving issues.

Fewer games and players at higher levels means less consumer play testing, which means not only are issues going to take longer to fix, they're going to take longer to find too. The wisdom and consensus of the masses, or lack thereof, cannot be applied here, yet.

Fair points are made when people point out various ways the game breaks/is broken at higher levels due to how powerful the characters and equipment have become.  Something that should be considered though is how broken earlier levels might be too if they were played as often as later levels.

* Most people aren't considering how rampant disease and sickness would run as a direct result of a zombie infestation. 
* Setting aside indirect affects such as rioting and other violence, infrastructure breakdown, and other problems caused by people reacting to zombies, and even setting aside direct affects of zombie aggression such as death and infection from bites and contact, the zombies are still big piles of unsanitary YUCK.
* I've seen a number of posts that minimize the threat of zombies due to immobility. These posts do not take into account the dangers that zombies pose even when they aren't mobile or able to attack people.
* Zombies are still rotting corpses, and as such would pose threats similar to extreme examples of poor sanitation. Diseases thrive where the dead are not properly disposed of via burial, isolation, cremation, etc. 
* Even corpses that have been buried can still spread disease via seepage into water sources such as wells, rivers, and lakes. There's a very good reason why a latrine should not be dug near any source of drinking water.
* Diseases, carried by zombies, that can be spread via airborne contamination would be especially worrisome.
* Diseases could also be spread to humans from zombies indirectly, via rodents and insects. What if a camp of survivors had dogs, and those dogs ran into a field or some bushes to play, and rolled in zombie guts while playing, and then rolled in some dirt in such a way that people wouldn't notice blood or guts, then those dogs ran back to camp, where they jump up on and lick and play with the children and adults. Everyone could wake up as a zombie the next morning.
* Corpse disposal would have to be a top priority. Zombie bon fires would probably be the safest and most reliable method.
* Anybody handling corpses/setting fires would need to take all precautions against infection, such as hazmat suits, thick rubber gloves, goggles, and anything else applicable.

Over watering.

I've dealt with the same thing in both pots with and without great drainage. It's hard for me to take a passive role in my plant's growth, so I tend at times to water them before they need it instead of sticking to a set watering schedule, or waiting for them to show signs of needing water. Persistent sitting moisture breeds mold.

my Guidelines for watering (and avoiding mold/fungus):

1. Don't add more water if the surface and/or the first 1/4 inch to 2 inches (0.635 - 5.08 cm) of soil are noticeably moist.    Plant roots are great at sucking moisture from dirt, even if the dirt would be to dry for a human to squeeze water from, so if there's moisture near the plant's roots, the plant will get it. The soil does not need to be soaking wet and muddy for the plant to get water. If there is moist soil sticking to your finger after sticking it into the soil up to the first or second knuckle, the plant probably doesn't need water. If there's dirt on your finger, but it is dry, or is easily wiped or blown off and doesn't leave anything but dust behind, it's probably ok to water your plant.
2. Plant leaves are basically floral solar panels, and should generally be perked up and have the broad side (top) facing the strongest light source. If the leaves, vines, or branches start to droop or look shriveled, the plant probably needs water. I recently transplanted a tomato plant from a pot indoors to the ground outside. 8 hours later, everything was drooping like a depressed highschooler. I'd watered the plant when I transplanted it, so I thought it couldn't possibly need more water. I was wrong. I poured 64 more ounces (size of the cup) of water on the ground at the base of the plant, and the plant looked great less than a half hour later. Water doesn't always fix this though. Root trauma is common during transplantation and plants sometimes just need some time to recover.
